intended_application: A supplier markets its new Agentic AI chart-review package, but the demonstrated system runs the same scheduled data refresh and preset chart rules as the existing BI workflow; it adds a one-shot caption draft without adaptive tool selection.
organization: A mid-sized United States financial-services firm with centralized business analytics, model-risk, information-security, and compliance functions.
industry_sector: Regulated financial services and internal management reporting.
business_need: Determine whether a newly branded package represents a significant process innovation or only a routine update before making disruption claims.
users_stakeholders: Business analysts, analytics managers, model-risk staff, compliance reviewers, information-security staff, executives who consume reports, and customers indirectly affected by management decisions.
adoption_posture: Conservative and risk-averse. The firm permits bounded pilots but requires evidence of reliability, access control, auditability, and named human decision ownership before broader adoption.
capabilities_constraints: The firm has an established BI stack, approved data repositories, experienced analysts, and security review processes. Constraints include sensitive data, legacy systems, limited agent-specific evaluation data, strict vendor review, and a prohibition on autonomous external publication.
risk_consequence_context: A fabricated claim, incorrect denominator, privacy breach, or misleading visual could affect executive decisions, regulatory obligations, and reputation. Drafts are reversible, but distribution of an incorrect report can have material consequences.
management_question: What innovation classification is defensible for this chart-review application, how could it alter value creation and the firm's business model, and how severe is the disruption over the next 12 months?
time_horizon: Decision now; assess exposure over the next 12 months.
additional_context:
Fictional analytical scenario, not an observed real-company deployment. The technology is defined as an LLM selecting or sequencing tools, reading results and adapting multi-step work, with human authority over release. The workflow is proposed, not yet in operational use. Evidence packet checked 2026-10-12:
S1 | OECD/Eurostat. (2018). Oslo Manual 2018: Guidelines for collecting, reporting and using data on innovation (4th ed.). OECD Publishing. | https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/oslo-manual-2018_9789264304604-en/full-report/component-7.html | Chapter 2, paragraphs 2.19-2.25; chapter 3, paragraphs 3.9-3.14, 3.56-3.69 | Support: Implementation distinguishes innovation from a concept or prototype; novelty can be relative to the firm, market or world. Routine changes are insufficient. | Limit: Does not supply a universal numeric threshold for breakthrough or forecast this fictional firm's outcome.
S2 | Yao, S., Zhao, J., Yu, D., Du, N., Shafran, I., Narasimhan, K., & Cao, Y. (2023). ReAct: Synergizing reasoning and acting in language models. ICLR. | https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.03629 | Abstract and method | Support: A language model can interleave reasoning and actions, use tools, observe outcomes and revise its plan. | Limit: The cited experiments do not measure chart-review accuracy, commercial demand or financial-services workflow performance.
S3 | Christensen, C. M., Raynor, M. E., & McDonald, R. (2015). What is disruptive innovation? Harvard Business Review, 93(12), 44-53. | https://www.hbs.edu/ris/Publication%20Files/McDonald_Rory_A04_What%20is%20Disruptive%20Innovation_182498a6-5391-4916-a38b-d14932db41a6.pdf | Sections on low-end/new-market footholds and disruption as a process | Support: Christensen-style disruption requires a market trajectory; technical novelty or a successful efficiency improvement alone does not establish it. | Limit: The course's broad creative-destruction lens can describe task displacement without establishing this narrower theory.
S4 | Brynjolfsson, E., Li, D., & Raymond, L. (2025). Generative AI at work. The Quarterly Journal of Economics, 140(2), 889-942. https://doi.org/10.1093/qje/qjae044 | https://academic.oup.com/qje/article/140/2/889/7990658 | Abstract and Introduction, sample and external-validity qualifications | Support: In one firm, AI-assisted customer-support workers had heterogeneous productivity effects; the reported average was 15% across 5,172 workers. | Limit: Human support agents are workers, not autonomous software agents. This is not chart-workflow evidence and does not establish employment, wage or business-model displacement.
S5 | Anthropic. (2024, October 22). Introducing computer use, a new Claude 3.5 Sonnet, and Claude 3.5 Haiku. | https://www.anthropic.com/news/3-5-models-and-computer-use | Computer use introduction and public beta limitations | Support: A vendor offered model-directed computer interaction through a public beta, documenting a commercialization pathway for tool-using AI. | Limit: A release announcement does not establish market-wide adoption, current product status, reliability or a new business model for the case organization.
Boundary-case override: supplier demonstration shows only fixed rules and one-shot text generation, not the operational agentic loop defined above. The package is proposed and no meaningful difference in review quality, process capabilities or business-model economics is evidenced. Only the supplier label claims novelty. The underlying ET family remains Agentic AI for the general analysis, but this supplied application may not instantiate it. The organization's current revenue model is not supplied.
